newsitem.title: INDIA: Thousands of Bombay workers mourn slain leader.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Bombay workers mourn slain leader.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of workers massed in Bombay's streets on Friday to mourn slain trade union leader Datta Samant, and a protest strike slowed traffic in India's normally bustling commercial capital.
Samant, 65, was shot dead in a city suburb on Thursday by four unidentified gunmen.
Trade unions called a general strike to protest the mafia-style killing that rocked India's labour movement, and fuelled speculation about the role of organised crime in Bombay.

Police brought in reinforcements to ensure Samant's funeral procession and the strike were relatively peaceful on a day already marked by heightened security for a visit by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Deve Gowda was to pay a courtesy call on Reserve Bank of India governor Chakravarty Rangarajan during his visit.
"We are not taking any chances," one police source said.

Samant's bullet-ridden body lay on blocks of ice covered with flowers and garlands, surrounded by family members in the office where he had practiced as a doctor for 30 years, while workers filed through to pay their last respects.

An unending flow of mourners trekked from railway stations to join hundreds of thousands of people, many of them wailing and weeping women, who gathered outside the office in Pant Nagar, a predominantly working-class residential area.
Workers carried flags showing a rising sun over a clenched fist, the symbol of the Kamgar Aghadi (Workers Front), the main union established by Samant, and banners lauding Samat.
"This man has sacrificed everything for workers including his life," one sobbing worker told Reuters.
Samant's unions represent nearly one million workers at more than 4,000 industrial units in and around Bombay and other parts of Maharashtra state.
Police said they suspected inter-union rivalry as the motive for the killing. Businessmen say organised crime has infiltrated trade unions in the city of 13 million people.
As the crowds gathered, police reported only a few isolated incidents of stone throwing in Bombay's northwest suburbs.

In central Bombay and it's eastern suburbs, where textile mills employing members of Samant's trade unions are concentrated, life was virtually paralysed with shops closed, and buses and taxis off the streets.
Shops in other areas were open although fewer buses and taxis were in use. Train services were normal.

Police said Samant and his son were travelling in a jeep when the attackers fired from a motor-rickshaw in the central suburb of Powai. Samant's son was unhurt but his chauffeur was seriously wounded.

A doctor who became a militant trade unionist, Samant took the spotlight in the early 1980s when he led a two-year strike by textile workers in Bombay. He later became a member of the Maharashtra state legislature and the national parliament.
